Thanks for this, and sorry for the slow response. I ran the proposed config against a clean checkout to see what it would actually gate on, and we have decided not to adopt codespell here. Sharing the numbers since they drove the decision.

On a fresh `git archive` of main, the config produces **52 hits across 22 files, of which exactly one is a real typo**:

| Token | Count | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `nin`, `nnumber`, `ndefined`, `ndoes` | 25 | false positive — `\n` escapes in the vendored `skills/bids/references/bids_schema.json` |
| `TRE` | 5 | Trusted Research Environment (DNAnexus) |
| `ACI` | 5 | domain acronym |
| `assignin` | 4 | a real MATLAB builtin |
| `ONS` | 3 | UK Office for National Statistics |
| `EDE`, `NED`, `HSI`, `Bloc`/`Blocs` | 6 | domain acronyms — NED is the NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database |
| `pre-selected`, `Re-using` | 3 | style preferences, not misspellings |
| **`questons`** | **1** | **genuine** |

So as submitted the check fails on merge and stays failing. That part is fixable — skipping the vendored schema and adding about 11 entries to `ignore-words-list` gets it to exit 0, which I verified locally.

The reason we are still passing: the corrected config catches a single typo across 150 skills, and the ignore list needed to get there is already 60+ entries heavily weighted toward scientific acronyms. This repo is nearly all domain vocabulary — gene symbols, instrument names, database acronyms, chemical abbreviations — so that list would grow with roughly every new skill, and the failure mode is a contributor blocked by a red check on a correctly-spelled term. That maintenance cost outweighs the defect rate we are seeing.

The `questons` typo is a real find and is being fixed separately, with credit to you. Genuinely appreciate the effort, and the `ignore-regex` for camelCase identifiers was a nice touch.

181.author: yarikoptic
181.last_developer_comment_body:
@yarikoptic Thanks for your work on this. It was useful to see how a tool such as codespell could be included in CI and obviously, by using it, you have helped us fix a number of typos. When it comes to this PR for adding it to the CI process I'm afraid we have decided not to include that but have moved the additional typos found in this PR to the other one. There is nothing wrong with the general idea but here are the reasons we don't want in include it at this point in time:

1. This repo is not likely to be very active and now that the identified typos have been fixed, there would be little benefit to including codespell in CI.
2. We want to avoid any additional maintenance overhead so if there isn't sufficient benefit we don't want to add new tools.
3. Lastly, as you suggested, it is hard to make this robust. Your regex was a good idea but it didn't catch multi-line text that ends with a language tag so it still made mistakes in non-English text. To maintain this tool in CI we would need to run it locally, identify cases it missed and modify the config. That diminishes the benefit of running it in CI.

Thanks again for your contribution and the improvements you have made to the quality of this repo.

2075.title: Add codespell to CI
2075.author: DimitriPapadopoulos
2075.last_developer_comment_body:
I definitely can understand not wanting to deter contributors if it runs in CI, given the chance of false positives. And if autofix is enabled, while pre-commit will abort the commit with a message to review the changes, which the contributor would then need to re-add and re-commit, I could certainly see the possibility of a contributor not carefully checking, especially if they weren't familiar with the workflow.

Instead of adding it as a hard requirement which gets installed on all platforms, CIs and locally, (regardless if the user actually wants to perform spell checking), and in the same environment as the build (potential for dep conflicts), why not just add the pre-commit hook with `hook-stage: manual`, and run it via `pre-commit run codespell` (perhaps with an alias in the `Makefile`, for completeness)? Pre-commit will then take care of installing it if/when it is needed in its own isolated environment with a consistent pinned version for all devs (with easy updates via `pre-commit autoupdate`), and it works cross-platform unlike relying solely on the Makefile.
